The bathroom incident may feel humiliating or upsetting to students because the scene shows segregation in an everyday setting. Part A: How Responses to Events Reveal Key Ideas (RI.6.3) (15 minutes)
Have students work in pairs to analyze the bathroom scene. Direct them to the section in Chapter 11 where Mary is told about the "colored bathroom" and the events that follow.

Reread the section of text in Chapter 11 that describes the bathroom incident. As you read, stop at the part of the text when Mary is directed to the "colored bathroom." Pay careful attention to the details that show how she responds. Use the 3-Column Chart to track the event, the response, and what key idea the response reveals.

I begin by identifying the event I’m focusing on, then pay close attention to how people respond to it. When Mary is told about the bathroom rule, she becomes furious—it’s clear she is not willing to accept it. Next, I look for textual evidence that shows this response: “Mary Jackson was angered—no, enraged—to have been confronted with such blatant

.” Then, I ask myself what key idea her response reveals. The text explains that this experience reduced her “from professional mathematician to second-class human being.” This evidence emphasizes how deeply the injustice affects her and highlights her strong sense of dignity and refusal to accept unfair treatment.
What event does Mary experience in Chapter 11?

Mary asks to use the bathroom and finds out that the nearest women’s bathroom was open to white women only. Because she was Black she was directed to the "colored bathroom" which was much farther away.
How does Mary respond to this event?
Mary responds by getting very angry and making it clear to others that this rule is unfair, unacceptable and she will not go along with it.
What key idea is revealed through this response?

Mary’s response reveals the injustice and inequality faced by Black women professionals at Langley. Her response connects to the larger ideas of prejudice and racism that Black women faced during this time.

Correct: This answer explains both the event and its meaning. It highlights Mary’s traits and shows how her response challenges the unfair assumption behind the rule.

Part B: Analyzing Mary’s Response to Events (RI.6.1) (15 minutes)

Students will use their 3-Column chart notes to draft a two-to-three-sentence explanation in response to the prompt. Remind them that this is not a full paragraph; it is a short analytical response that still needs evidence and explanation.
We are going to use the RACE strategy to analyze how a character’s response to events reveals key ideas.
Write a 2-3 sentence explanation that responds to the following question. How does Mary’s response to the bathroom rule show that she is not afraid to challenge the injustice of segregation?

how the evidence supports the key idea that is revealed through the character’s response.

Mary Jackson, a courageous engineer in training, refuses to treat the "colored bathroom" rule as acceptable. In the moment when she is directed to a separate restroom, her angry response shows both courage and

because she recognizes that the rule is based on prejudice, not fairness and is not afraid to express her anger. In Chapter 11, when Mary is told about the “colored bathrooms”, she didn’t just accept it, she “stormed off to look on her own” and later feels “enraged” by the incident. This response reveals that Mary rejects being treated as less than equal and is not afraid to challenge the injustice of segregation.
Let’s identify where the sample response restates the question, answers the question, cites text evidence, and explains what the evidence means.

The first sentence restates and answers the question by explaining what the bathroom incident shows about Mary Jackson. The response cites evidence from Chapter 11, including the moment when she cannot use the restroom and “stormed off to look on her own.” The final sentence explains how her response shows
by highlighting her anger and refusal to accept unfair treatment.
